title: Dates and time
summary: DateOnly, TimeOnly and weekday arithmetic, and a clock you can pass in, so Sidekick knows that yesterday on a Monday was Friday.

steps.title: An assistant lives on dates
body: Your Sidekick talks about time constantly: *yesterday* in the standup, *this week* in the chart, *due in 2 days*,
*5 min ago*. .NET gives each idea its own type, so you never carry a time of day you do not need:
| Type | Holds | Example |
| `DateOnly` | a calendar day | a due date, "yesterday" |
| `TimeOnly` | a time of day | 09:30 in `sk log 3 09:30-10:15` |
| `DateTime` | both | when a timer started |
| `TimeSpan` | a length of time | 1 h 25 min |
```csharp
var due = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30);          // year, month, day
var start = new TimeOnly(9, 30);
DateTime at = due.ToDateTime(start);           // 2026-11-30 09:30
DateOnly day = DateOnly.FromDateTime(at);      // back to the day
The trap this lesson removes: on a **Monday**, "yesterday" in a standup means **Friday**.

steps.prompt: A task's due date has no time of day: it is due *on* 30 November. Which type should `TaskItem.Due` be?
steps.explain: `DateOnly` says exactly "a day", so nobody wonders whether 00:00 or 23:59 is meant, and `?` says a task may have no due date at all.

steps.title: Arithmetic on days
body: ```csharp fragment
var d = new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25);   // a Wednesday
d.DayOfWeek                            // DayOfWeek.Wednesday
(int)d.DayOfWeek                       // 3   (Sunday is 0, Monday 1, ... Saturday 6)
new DateOnly(2026, 12, 1).DayNumber - d.DayNumber   // 6: days between two dates
d.ToString("ddd d MMM")                // "Wed 25 Nov"
`DayNumber` counts days since 1 January of year 1, so subtracting two of them gives a whole number of days with no
time zones or hours to worry about. `AddDays` with a negative number goes back.
A Monday-based week start: how many days back is Monday? For Monday 0, Tuesday 1, ... Sunday 6. That is
`((int)d.DayOfWeek + 6) % 7`, because Sunday is 0 in .NET.

steps.explain: 25 November 2026 is a Wednesday; five days later is Monday 30th. There are 6 days to 1 December. Three days back is Sunday 22nd.

steps.title: Late returns
prompt: A library charges for late books. Write two methods:
- `static int DaysLate(DateOnly due, DateOnly returned)`: how many days after `due` the book came back; `0` if it was on time or early.
- `static bool IsWeekend(DateOnly day)`: `true` on Saturday and Sunday.
```text
DaysLate(30 Nov, 3 Dec) -> 3      DaysLate(30 Nov, 28 Nov) -> 0
IsWeekend(Sat 28 Nov) -> true     IsWeekend(Mon 30 Nov) -> false
starter: static int DaysLate(DateOnly due, DateOnly returned)
solution: static int DaysLate(DateOnly due, DateOnly returned)
hints: `returned.DayNumber - due.DayNumber` is the number of days between them.
template: {{CODE}}
Dojo.Eq("3 days late", 3, DaysLate(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30), new DateOnly(2026, 12, 3)));
Dojo.Eq("early is 0", 0, DaysLate(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 28)));
Dojo.Eq("on the day is 0", 0, DaysLate(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30), new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30)));
Dojo.Eq("across a year end", 5, DaysLate(new DateOnly(2026, 12, 29), new DateOnly(2027, 1, 3)));
Dojo.Check("Saturday is weekend", IsWeekend(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 28)));
Dojo.Check("Sunday is weekend", IsWeekend(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 29)));
Dojo.Check("Monday is not", !IsWeekend(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 30)));
Dojo.Check("Friday is not", !IsWeekend(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 27)));
steps.explain: Subtracting `DayNumber`s never trips over month lengths, leap years or year ends: it is just counting days.

steps.prompt: Complete `WeekStart`: the Monday of the week that `day` is in (Sunday belongs to the week that started the Monday before).
steps.explain: For Monday `(1 + 6) % 7` is 0 days back; for Sunday `(0 + 6) % 7` is 6 days back.

steps.title: Never ask the wall clock inside tested code
body: If `Today()` called `DateTime.Now`, a test of "due today" would pass on Tuesday and fail on Wednesday. The clock
is a **hidden input**. So Sidekick takes the clock as a parameter, a **seam**: .NET's `TimeProvider`.
```csharp
static DateOnly Today(TimeProvider clock) => DateOnly.FromDateTime(clock.GetLocalNow().DateTime);
Today(TimeProvider.System);            // the real app: the real clock
class FixedClock : TimeProvider        // the tests: a clock that never moves
readonly DateTimeOffset now;
public FixedClock(DateTimeOffset now) { this.now = now; }
public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => now;
public override TimeZoneInfo LocalTimeZone => TimeZoneInfo.Utc;
`GetLocalNow()` is built on the two members a fake overrides: the current UTC instant and the time zone. Your `sk`
host passes `TimeProvider.System`; your tests pass a `FixedClock`. Same code, both worlds.

steps.prompt: Match each piece to its job.
pairs: the real clock, passed in by the sk host
the method a fake clock overrides
now, in the clock's own time zone
a hidden input that makes tests flaky

steps.prompt: A test checks `IsDueSoon(task)` for a task due on 25 November. It passed yesterday and fails today, with no code changes. What is the most likely cause?
options: `IsDueSoon` reads `DateTime.Now` instead of a clock passed in
The compiler cached an old build
steps.explain: The only thing that changed is the date. Pass the clock in, and the test pins it to one moment forever.

steps.title: Sidekick: dates that know about weekends
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk standup` needs "yesterday", `sk week` needs "this Monday", and `sk` itself prints
"started 5 min ago". Write four methods:
1. `static DateOnly Today(TimeProvider clock)`: today's date by the given clock (`GetLocalNow()`).
2. `static DateOnly PreviousWorkday(DateOnly day)`: the workday before `day`: Monday, Saturday and Sunday all go
back to Friday; any other day goes back one day. (A `switch` on `day.DayOfWeek`.)
3. `static DateOnly WeekStart(DateOnly day)`: the Monday of `day`'s week.
4. `static string Ago(DateTime then, DateTime now)`:
- `then` after `now`: `in the future`
- under a minute: `just now`; under an hour: `5 min ago`; under a day: `3 h ago` (whole numbers, rounded down)
- otherwise count calendar days between the two dates: 1 is `yesterday`, more is `4 days ago`.
```text
PreviousWorkday(Mon 23 Nov) -> Fri 20 Nov        WeekStart(Sun 29 Nov) -> Mon 23 Nov
Ago(24 Nov 08:00, 25 Nov 09:00) -> yesterday     Ago(24 Nov 18:00, 25 Nov 09:00) -> 15 h ago
The tests pass a fake clock fixed at 25 November 2026, 09:00 UTC.
starter: static string Ago(DateTime then, DateTime now)
solution: static DateOnly PreviousWorkday(DateOnly day) => day.DayOfWeek switch
static string Ago(DateTime then, DateTime now)
hints: `day.DayOfWeek switch { DayOfWeek.Monday => day.AddDays(-3), DayOfWeek.Sunday => day.AddDays(-2), _ => day.AddDays(-1) }` (Saturday minus one is Friday).
In `Ago`, `TimeSpan span = now - then;` then test `span.TotalMinutes < 1`, `span.TotalHours < 1`, `span.TotalDays < 1` in that order; for days use `DayNumber`s of the two dates.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoClock = new DojoClock(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 25, 9, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
Dojo.Eq("Today reads the clock it is given", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25), Today(dojoClock));
Dojo.Eq("late in the evening is still today", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25), Today(new DojoClock(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 11, 25, 23, 30, 0, TimeSpan.Zero))));
Dojo.Eq("Wednesday -> Tuesday", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 24), PreviousWorkday(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25)));
Dojo.Eq("Tuesday -> Monday", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23), PreviousWorkday(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 24)));
Dojo.Eq("Monday -> Friday", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 20), PreviousWorkday(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23)));
Dojo.Eq("Sunday -> Friday", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 20), PreviousWorkday(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 22)));
Dojo.Eq("Saturday -> Friday", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 20), PreviousWorkday(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 21)));
Dojo.Eq("Monday 1 Dec 2025 -> Friday 28 Nov", new DateOnly(2025, 11, 28), PreviousWorkday(new DateOnly(2025, 12, 1)));
Dojo.Eq("WeekStart of a Wednesday is Monday", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23), WeekStart(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 25)));
Dojo.Eq("WeekStart of a Monday is itself", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23), WeekStart(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23)));
Dojo.Eq("WeekStart of a Sunday is the Monday before", new DateOnly(2026, 11, 23), WeekStart(new DateOnly(2026, 11, 29)));
var dojoNow = new DateTime(2026, 11, 25, 9, 0, 0);
Dojo.Eq("30 seconds", "just now", Ago(dojoNow.AddSeconds(-30), dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("5 minutes", "5 min ago", Ago(dojoNow.AddMinutes(-5), dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("3 hours", "3 h ago", Ago(dojoNow.AddHours(-3), dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("15 hours, across midnight", "15 h ago", Ago(new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 18, 0, 0), dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("25 hours", "yesterday", Ago(new DateTime(2026, 11, 24, 8, 0, 0), dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("5 days", "5 days ago", Ago(new DateTime(2026, 11, 20, 10, 0, 0), dojoNow));
Dojo.Eq("a time after now", "in the future", Ago(dojoNow.AddMinutes(1), dojoNow));
class DojoClock : TimeProvider
readonly DateTimeOffset now;
public DojoClock(DateTimeOffset now) { this.now = now; }
public override DateTimeOffset GetUtcNow() => now;
public override TimeZoneInfo LocalTimeZone => TimeZoneInfo.Utc;
steps.explain: Everything that depends on "now" takes the clock as a parameter, so every rule here is tested at a fixed moment, and the real `sk` passes `TimeProvider.System`. Weekend logic lives in one place: the standup, the week chart and the streak all call these.
